**Incident Summary — Checkout Endpoint Outage, Friday**

**Overview**

The checkout endpoint was degraded or fully unavailable for approximately two hours on Friday, beginning shortly after the 14:10 deployment and resolved at 16:15 following a rollback to the previous release. Customer-facing impact was limited to checkout; browse, search, and account endpoints remained healthy throughout. Roughly 4,100 checkout attempts returned 502 or timed out during the window, and a smaller number of orders entered a partially written state that the data team has since reconciled.

**Rollback**

On-call was paged at 14:22 by the error-rate alert and began investigating immediately. The first fifteen minutes were spent confirming that the failure correlated with the deployment rather than an upstream payment provider issue. Once the correlation was clear, the team initiated a rollback to the prior build at 15:48; propagation across all regions completed by 16:07, and error rates returned to baseline by 16:15. The rollback itself executed cleanly and required no manual intervention beyond the standard approval step.

The main delay was not the rollback mechanism but the decision to trigger it. Our runbook does not define a hard time limit for diagnosis before reverting, so the team continued investigating well past the point where a revert would have shortened impact.

**What the Logs Showed**

Queue latency told the clearest story. Under normal conditions, the order-processing queue holds messages for a median of 40 to 60 milliseconds, with a p99 under 400 milliseconds. Beginning at 14:14, median dwell time climbed steadily, passing two seconds by 14:30 and peaking near 47 seconds around 15:20. Depth grew in parallel, reaching just over 190,000 messages before the rollback allowed consumers to drain the backlog.

The new release introduced a synchronous inventory verification call inside the consumer loop. That call added between 300 and 900 milliseconds per message, which pushed effective consumer throughput below the incoming message rate. Once arrival exceeded processing capacity, the queue grew without bound, and upstream request handlers began timing out while awaiting acknowledgment. Nothing in the code path failed outright, which is why our health checks stayed green and why the initial investigation looked in the wrong direction. Load testing in staging had used a fixture set roughly a twentieth of production volume, so the throughput ceiling never appeared.

**Changes Before the Next Release**

We are adding a queue-dwell-time alert that fires when median latency exceeds one second for three consecutive minutes, which would have paged us roughly eight minutes earlier and pointed directly at the responsible subsystem. Alongside that, the deployment runbook will specify a thirty-minute diagnosis window: if a suspected deployment-related incident is not understood and mitigated within that period, the default action becomes rollback, with investigation continuing afterward against the reverted build.

On the engineering side, the inventory verification call is being reworked to run asynchronously with a bounded timeout so a slow dependency cannot stall the consumer loop. We are also rebuilding the staging load profile to mirror production peak volume, and adding a pre-release check that measures consumer throughput against projected arrival rate and blocks promotion if the margin falls below thirty percent.

Owners and target dates for each item are tracked in the incident ticket. A follow-up review is scheduled for Wednesday.

Indoor light can look normal to your eye, but your eye can adapt to dim light in a way that no recording chip can. A lamp‑lit room might carry only a tiny fraction of the light available outdoor at midday. To gather enough light, your gear will hold the exposure open longer, and the exposure time (in effect, how long light can enter, marked on the dial in fraction form) might reach 1/15 or beyond. During that interval, any wobble in your hand, or any motion in front of you, will paint blur into the picture. That blur can tell you the interval ran long — nothing about the optic went wrong.

The aperture, the round opening in the optic labeled by f‑number, will govern how much light can pour in at once. A lower f‑number, like f/1.8, will mark a wider opening: far more light than f/8, which can cut the exposure interval enough to kill the blur. The trade‑off: a wide opening will narrow the depth of field, hence only a thin band in front of and behind the aimed point can land clear. A face might land clear while an ear might go blurry.

A tripod will cure one kind of blur, not both. Locked down, the gear cannot wobble, hence even a long exposure can come out clean. But a tripod will do nothing about a kid mid‑jump, a wagging tail, or an arm in motion; that motion will blur anyway. Hence the rule of thumb: mount the gear when the meal, the room, or the architecture can hold entirely quiet. For a child at play or a pet indoor, no tripod can help; you want a wider opening, more light in the room, extra amplification in the gear, and 1/125 or briefer on the exposure timer.

Great question! The dark afternoon isn't weather at all — it's the season doing its thing.

Here's the difference. Weather is what's happening outside right now, today. Rain, sunshine, wind, snow, fog: those can change by the hour. You might need a raincoat in the morning and sunglasses by lunchtime. Weather is a bit like your mood — it shifts.

A season is much bigger and slower. A season is a long stretch of the year, about three months, and it sets the general pattern that the weather plays inside. Winter, spring, summer, autumn. A season doesn't change from hour to hour; it creeps along so gently you barely notice until suddenly the mornings are frosty.

Now, why the early dark? That's a season thing, not a weather thing. Our planet is tilted, a bit like a spinning top leaning to one side. As Earth travels its long loop around the sun over a whole year, that lean means our part of the world sometimes tips toward the sun and sometimes tips away. When we're tipped toward it, we get long summer days where it's still bright at bedtime. When we're tipped away, the sun takes a low, short path across the sky and slips away early — hence dark at four.

So a cloudy day can make the afternoon gloomy, and that's weather. But the sun genuinely setting at four o'clock? That's winter, and no amount of clear sky will change it.

The cheerful part: it doesn't last. Around late December the days quietly start stretching again, a minute or two at a time, until you're back to playing outside after dinner.

Picture a Saturday shift stacking shelves at the supermarket. The wage lands in a bank each week, and a slice — say £10 — stays there rather than getting spent.

After a year, the savings sit at £500, and the bank pays 5% interest each year. That first year adds £25, leaving £525.

Here is the clever bit. In year 2, the 5% isn't calculated against £500. It is calculated against £525 — the initial stash plus its added interest. That yields £26.25, leaving £551.25. Year 3 pays 5% against that bigger figure: £27.56, ending at £578.81. Interest is earning interest. Each year the base is bigger, the added slice is bigger, and it never quits.

Early years feel dull, and that is the sneaky part; the big gains arrive at the far end. Leave that £500 sitting there, adding never a single penny extra, and at 5% each year it will reach past £4,400 by age 61. Nine times the initial stash, gained while asleep.

The same maths bites in reverse. A credit card charging 25% each year lets a debt breed fresh debt, week after week, unless the card is cleared fast. Same engine, aimed the wrong way.

That is why starting a savings habit at 16 beats starting at 30 with triple the wage. The earliest pennies get the greatest run, and every year in that run is bigger than the year that camein

That jolt under your wheel came from a deliberate gap in the road, and from the gap doing exactly what it ought to do.

A bridge deck cannot keep one fixed length. Concrete and metal grow longer in heat and draw inward in cold. Per meter, the change might look tiny; over a long deck, it can add up to a hand-width or more between a frigid January night and a broiling July afternoon.

Give that motion nowhere to go and it will turn into force. Force with no relief can buckle a roadway, crack a pier, or tear a deck away from the concrete block anchoring either end. The remedy: an intentional opening at either end of the deck, and between one deck panel and the next, wide enough to take up a full year of coming and going. An engineer will call it a movement joint. The gap will handle the flexing under a loaded truck, the nudge of hard wind, and any tremor in the earth, too.

A bare hole in the pavement would be no gift to a driver, and no gift to your wheel, and thu the opening will wear a cap: interlocking metal toothwork, comb meeting comb, or a thick rubber pad ribbed like an accordion. Either kind can carry your load while yielding to the daily creep of the deck.

What you felt going over it, then, add up to metal, rubber, a hairline of daylight, and a change in texture. None of them can match the calm of unbroken pavement. Read the bump not for a flaw in the road, but for a bridge breathing, and for the builder who left it room to breathe.

**To:** All staff and contractors, Ashgrove House
**From:** Facilities and Safety Team
**Date:** 12 March
**Subject:** Revised fire-drill and evacuation procedure — effective 1 April

The evacuation procedure for the building has been revised following the annual fire risk review. The main change concerns the lifts and the arrangements for anyone who normally relies on them. Please read this memo in full before the next drill, which is scheduled for the morning of 8 April.

**What stays the same**

The alarm signal is unchanged: a continuous ringing tone means evacuate immediately. The assembly point remains the paved area beside the visitor car park, on the far side of the barrier. Fire wardens will continue to sweep their designated floors and report headcounts to the incident controller at the assembly point. Nobody should re-enter the building until the incident controller gives permission.

**What changes for lift users**

Under the old procedure, the lifts returned to the ground floor and shut down as soon as the alarm sounded, and staff who could not use the stairs waited on their floor until the fire service arrived. That arrangement has ended.

The north lift has now been upgraded to an evacuation lift with a protected shaft, an independent power supply and a firefighter override key. When the alarm sounds, this lift will travel to the ground floor and remain there under warden control. It may then be used, on the instruction of a fire warden only, to bring people down from the upper floors. The south lift is not part of this arrangement and will continue to shut down at ground level for the duration of any alarm.

If you would ordinarily use a lift to leave the building, do not wait at your desk. Make your way to the refuge point on your floor, which is the protected lobby beside the north lift on levels two, three and four. Each refuge point has a two-way communication panel connected to the ground-floor control position. Press the call button, state your floor and the number of people with you, and stay in the refuge until a warden reaches you or you are directed into the evacuation lift. The refuge areas are fire-resisting enclosures and are a safe place to wait for the short period involved.

Anyone else should continue to use the stairs. Please keep clear of the north lift lobby so that wardens and evacuation-lift users can move through it without obstruction.

**Personal emergency evacuation plans**

Every member of staff who may need assistance, whether because of a mobility, sensory, cognitive or temporary condition such as an injury, should hold a personal emergency evacuation plan. These plans are being rewritten to reflect the new lift arrangements. If you already hold one, your line manager will contact you before 25 March to agree the revised version. If you do not hold one and think you may need help to leave the building, please contact the Facilities and Safety Team directly; there is no need to go through your manager, and the conversation will be treated in confidence.

Visitors and contractors who may need assistance should be identified at reception on arrival, and the host is responsible for informing the floor warden.

**Warden responsibilities**

Floor wardens should familiarise themselves with the location of the refuge points and the operating instructions for the evacuation lift, which are displayed inside the north lift lobby on each level. A short briefing session will be held in the third-floor training room at 10am on 27 March, repeated at 2pm the same day. Attendance is required for all wardens and deputies.

**Questions**

Please direct any questions to the Facilities and Safety Team on extension 4120. A copy of the full revised procedure has been posted on the intranet under Building Safety, and printed copies are held at reception and in each floor lobby.

**Why That Same Dip in the Road Turns Into a Pond Every Autumn**

If you've ever slowed to a crawl at the bottom of that hill after a night of heavy rain, you're not imagining things. It really is always the same fifty yards, and there's a reason for it that has very little to do with bad luck.

Start with the shape of the land. Water doesn't wander; it takes the cheapest route downhill, every single time. Roads were often laid along the flattest, easiest ground available, which is frequently the very bottom of a natural bowl or an old stream line. So when rain falls across a wide area of fields, gardens and rooftops, a surprising volume of it converges on one low point — and that low point happens to be tarmac.

Then there's what autumn does to the ground. Through summer, soil behaves a bit like a dry sponge left on the draining board: the first splash beads off, but it eventually soaks up a fair amount. By October, that sponge is already saturated from weeks of steady damp. Fresh rain has nowhere to go but sideways, across the surface, downhill, into the dip.

Leaves are the third piece of it. A gully grate can swallow a remarkable amount of water until roughly a dozen wet sycamore leaves plaster themselves across the bars. After that it swallows almost nothing. The drain isn't broken and it isn't undersized; it's simply wearing a lid made of leaf litter, and the wind fits a new one every few hours during a gale.

Add to this the slow creep of hard surfaces. Every extension, patio, driveway and new access road in the catchment sends a little more water to the street rather than letting it soak away. None of these changes matters much on its own. Collectively, over twenty or thirty years, they can turn a puddle into a genuine hazard.

Finally, drains are designed to a standard, not to perfection. Engineers size pipes for a storm of a certain severity, because building for the worst conceivable downpour would cost more than any council could justify. When a heavier storm arrives, the system does exactly what it was designed to do — it fills up and overflows at the lowest point.

What actually helps is unglamorous: keeping the gullies cleared before the leaves fall rather than after, making sure roadside ditches haven't been filled in or blocked by fencing, and reporting standing water with a date and a photograph so there's a record when funding decisions are made. If you own land uphill of the dip, letting a corner stay rough and boggy does more good than you'd think, because every litre held back is a litre that doesn't arrive all at once.

The flood isn't a mystery. It's geography, a wet sponge, a handful of leaves and a few decades of small changes, all arriving at the same address on the same rainy Tuesday.

That steam is a good sign — it means your heap is working properly.

**What's making the heat**

The warmth isn't coming from the sun or from any chemical reaction in the plant material itself. It's coming from microbes: billions of bacteria and fungi eating their way through your grass clippings, kitchen scraps and leaves. Like any living thing, they burn fuel to grow and reproduce, and like any engine, they throw off waste heat while doing it. One microbe produces a vanishingly small amount. A few billion in a wheelbarrow's worth of material produce enough to raise the temperature dramatically.

**Why the middle and not the edges**

The centre of the heap is insulated on all sides by the material around it. Heat generated there has nowhere to escape quickly, so it accumulates. The outer few inches are losing warmth to the air as fast as it's produced, which is why the surface can feel cool while the core is too hot to hold your hand in.

Size matters for this reason. A heap smaller than about a cubic metre struggles to hold its heat and tends to stay lukewarm. Yours is clearly big enough.

**The temperature stages**

A well-built heap moves through phases. It starts with ordinary microbes working at ambient temperature. Within a day or two they've warmed things enough that a different crowd takes over — thermophiles, heat-loving organisms that thrive between 45 and 70°C. These are the ones responsible for the steam. They work fast and hard for a week or two, then run short of easily digestible food and die back. The heap cools, and slower fungi and worms move in for the long finishing stage.

**What the heat does for you**

Sustained temperatures above roughly 55°C kill most weed seeds and many plant pathogens. This is the main reason gardeners chase a hot heap rather than settling for a slow cold pile. It also speeds decomposition enormously — hot composting can finish in a couple of months where a cold heap takes a year.

**What to do now**

Check the core with a compost thermometer or a metal rod left in for a few minutes. If it's climbing past 70°C, the microbes start cooking themselves and the process stalls, so turn the heap to release heat. Otherwise, wait until the temperature drops noticeably, then turn it to bring the cooler outer material into the middle. You'll often get a second heat spike afterwards.

Keep it damp, roughly as wet as a wrung-out sponge. Dry heaps stall, sodden ones go airless and start to smell. If you want to push the heat higher next time, add more nitrogen-rich green material and make sure everything is chopped reasonably small.

output: Those orange-tinted prints from the 1970s are not dirty or badly stored so much as chemically worn out: colour photographs of that era build their image from three layers of organic dye — cyan, magenta and yellow — and these dyes do not age at the same rate. The cyan layer, especially in the mass-market papers used through the late 60s and 70s, was the least stable of the three, so it faded first under the slow attack of light, warmth and humidity. Take away the cyan and you are left with magenta plus yellow, which together read as red-orange, which is why faces, skies and grass all drift toward the same pinkish tangerine cast. Prints kept in a warm loft, a damp cupboard or a sunlit frame will have gone furthest, while ones pressed shut in an album or slipped into a drawer often keep more of their original balance, and Kodachrome slides from the same years may look almost untouched because their dyes were formed by a different process. The shift is permanent in the print itself, but a scan can usually recover a surprising amount by boosting what little cyan information remains, so it is worth digitising the worst offenders rather than discarding them, and storing the rest somewhere cool, dry and dark to slow what fading is left.

An expert report on the property will not tell you what the home might be worth. Your lender will care about that number, and will pay for a valuation to protect their own money. The report you pay for will do a very different job. It will look behind the paint. Damp in a corner, a roof near the end of a working life, wiring laid down half a century ago, a crack that might mean movement in the brickwork, a tree root creeping toward the drain. Little of that will jump out on a cheerful twenty-minute viewing. What you get back will be either calm, or a lever to renegotiate the price, or the clarity to walk away.

On completion day the money will travel in one direction and the key in the other. Your lawyer will end the balance of the agreed figure to the lawyer acting for the vendor, made up of your mortgage advance topped up by whatever you add from your own account, after taking account of the money already handed over at exchange. Out of your own pocket will come the tax due on land, the fee for your legal help, any fee the lender might charge for arranging the loan, the charge for putting your name on the title, cover for the building from the moment of exchange onward, and the bill from the removal firm. The vendor will look after the fee owed to the agent who marketed the home, will pay their own lawyer, and will clear any mortgage left on the property out of the money coming in. You will hand nothing directly to the vendor. Everything will travel through the lawyer acting for each party.

The timetable will move around, and the culprit will rarely be any one party. Until contract exchange, nothing will bind either buyer or vendor, and every link in a chain of linked move will depend on every other link. One mortgage offer late in coming, one query from the council about a road widening or an old planning permit, one lawyer away for a week, one family up the chain waiting on a probate matter, and the whole line will wait too. Add a lender wanting one more piece of paper at the eleventh hour, and a date pencilled in for April can drift to June. A drift like that need not mean trouble. It will mean only that many people, each with a plan of their own, have to land on one morning together. Keep your money where you can reach it quickly, reply to your lawyer on the day they write to you, and book the removal van later than you might like.

Congratulations on your buy. Skipping stitching is a top complaint with any stitching unit, and it almost always points to a small fault that you can put right on your own worktop, so try not to worry that you got saddld with a dud.

Start by thinking about what must occur for a stitch to form. That sharp point drops down through your cloth, hits bottom of its swing, and starts to lift. In that first tiny lift, friction from your cloth holds top cotton back, so a small loop puffs out at a flank of that shaft. A rotating hook, spinning in sync with all this, must swoop in and snag that loop at that instant, hauling it around cotton spooling off your bobbin. If no loop puffs out, or if that hook is not passing by at that split instant, nothing is caught, and you obtain a gap in your row: a skip.

Most skips fall back on that sharp point up top. A blunt or crooked point will push cloth down and not stab through it, so that loop forms wrong or not at all. A point sitting too high in its clamp, or spun half a turn round, will stow that loop out of that hook's path. And not all points suit all cloth: knits, vinyl and slippy fabric want a particular point, so a point built for plain cotton will skip on any cloth with spring in it. Bin any point you did not install yourself, as you cannot know what a past custodian did to it, and points go blunt without looking blunt.

Cotton path is culprit two. String your unit up with that foot up, always, so top cotton drops down into its tautness disks; string it up with that foot down and cotton floats past those disks, which brings slack, and slack cotton forms a loop too floppy for that hook to snag. Wind your bobbin smooth and flat, and drop it into its housing spinning in a right rotation, as its handbook shows.

How cloth runs counts too. If you tug or push cloth along, you can pull that shaft off its path by a hair, and it will not hit its slot at that vital instant. Thin or floppy cloth can also flap up and down with that point, blocking any loop from forming; a shim of stabilising cloth or thin card, torn away at a finish, will stop that. Backing off from full throttl by half also brings good luck.

If you dust out lint, drop oil into all spots your handbook calls for, install a virgin point of a right sort, string it all up from scratch, and skips still occur, timing is your last suspect: that hook and that shaft simply fall out of sync, possibly from a crash into a pin or a knock in transit. That is a shop job, and not a costly job.

So work in that mind: a fully unworn point first, cotton path and bobbin fitting than, cloth handling third, a shop only if all of that fails. Most folks who buy a unit unfamiliar to thm find that a virgin point sorts it out in a flash.

A heat pump works because even chilly outdoor air holds a great deal of thermal energy. The challenge is getting that energy to flow into a warmer house. Heat naturally moves from hot to cold so the machine uses a circulating fluid called a refrigerant to reverse the usual direction.

Outside sits a coil where the refrigerant arrives as a very cold low pressure liquid. Because it is colder than the outdoor air the air warms it and the liquid boils into vapor. A fan pushes outdoor air across the coil to speed up this exchange. The refrigerant has now absorbed heat from air that feels freezing to us.

Next a compressor squeezes that vapor. Compressing a gas raises both its pressure and its temperature so the refrigerant leaves the compressor much hotter than the indoor air.

The hot vapor then travels to a coil inside the house. Indoor air blown across this coil is cooler than the refrigerant so heat flows into the room and the vapor condenses back into a liquid. Ducts or radiators or a fan unit spread that warmth through the building.

Finally the liquid passes through an expansion valve. Dropping the pressure makes it very cold once more and it returns outdoors to begin the cycle again.

The payoff is efficiency. Electricity goes mostly toward running the compressor and the fans rather than toward creating heat directly so a good unit can deliver three or four units of warmth for every unit of electricity it draws. Performance does fall as outdoor temperatures sink because the refrigerant must bridge a wider temperature gap. Even so modern cold climate models still gather useful heat well below freezing.

Buying a flat in this way is not fully buying land or bricks. It is buying a right to occupy that flat for a long but known span such as 125 annual turns. A landlord holds full outright rights to all of that land and to that building as a whole.

That span shrinks daily. At its finish your right stops and it all falls back to your landlord. So prior to signing anything find out how many annual turns still run. Around 900 is grand. Anything dropping down towards 80 starts to look risky and a bank might not grant a loan on it. Adding additional duration to a short span costs a lot of cash. In law you can also join with additional flat occupants in your block and buy out your landlord's rights as a group.

You will normally pay two ongoing sums. A small annual sum simply for holding land plus a much bigger annual bill for communal work such as insuring your block and washing halls and fixing a roof. Ask what such bills add up to right now and if any big work is coming up soon.

Your contract will also hold many conditions. It might block dogs or bar loud music at night or stop you knocking down walls without your landlord signing off first.

Instruct a solicitor to go through all small print prior to buying. Two vital questions to ask. How many annual turns still run and how much do communal bills cost? A flat with a long span still to run and low annual bills is not much of a worry. A flat with a short span is a big warning sign.
